title: Chloe M. Nash, PhD
text:
About
Hello! I’m Chloe, an evolutionary ichthyologist fascinated by how marine fish diversity has evolved and what shapes it today. My research explores how evolutionary history, geography, and ecology interact to shape the diversity, distribution, and connectivity of fishes across space and time. I combine fieldwork, museum collections, genomics, and comparative biology to investigate these questions, from the evolutionary relationships among species to the processes shaping populations and communities. I’m especially interested in connecting the evolutionary history of fishes with the ecological and environmental factors that influence where they live and how they diversify. When I’m not working with fish, I’m usually happiest in diving in the water, exploring new cafes, and listening to live music!

title: Chloe M. Nash, PhD
text:
Current research


Biogeography and Community Composition
Why do fish occur where they do? I use comparative biogeography, species distributions, evolutionary history, and ecological traits to understand the processes shaping the composition and geographic diversity of marine fish communities.











Genomic connectivity
Why are some marine fish populations more connected than others? I use comparative population genomics to investigate dispersal, connectivity, and demographic processes across species, with the goal of understanding how connectivity shapes population resilience.





Phylogenetics
How has evolutionary history shaped marine fish diversity? I use molecular phylogenies and comparative methods to investigate diversification, biogeography, and the evolution of ecological and morphological traits.

title: Fieldwork
text:
Fieldwork keeps my research grounded in what fishes do and where they live. I collect specimens, record behavior, survey communities, and document habitats using SCUBA, snorkeling, and freediving.
The people involved are an important part of that work. Fishers, local researchers, fisheries cooperatives, and marine-station staff bring knowledge that helps me choose sites, understand observations, and think of questions I might otherwise miss. I work to keep these relationships useful beyond a single trip, with clear arrangements for collecting, specimen care, data use, recognition, and sharing results.
I am an AAUS Scientific Diver and NAUI Divemaster with more than 500 logged dives. Planning around local conditions, communicating clearly, and considering everyone’s experience are central to how I organize fieldwork.

title: Fieldwork
text:
Ryukyu Islands | 2023 to present





Fieldwork in Okinawa




Fish populations and reef communities
OIST has given me a base for working across the Ryukyus. I designed a comparative project to investigate how fishes are connected among islands and whether species show similar patterns along the Kuroshio pathway.
Collecting combines visits to local fish markets with targeted spearfishing on SCUBA and while freediving, working with fishers and fisheries cooperatives. The resulting specimens, tissues, and locality records support genomic, morphological, and taxonomic projects.
A related part of my work uses unattended cameras to record fish communities. At Diamond Beach in Seragaki, Okinawa, the cameras captured assemblages across seagrass, rubble, and coral habitats.

The project brought together field notes, locality records, preserved specimens, and mitochondrial sequences to investigate differences within and between island groups. It was an early introduction to questions I still enjoy working on: how does a fish’s association with a habitat relate to its geographic and genetic history?

title: Fieldwork
text:
What happens after a trip?
Much of the work continues after collecting. Specimens need preparation and cataloging, tissues need reliable labels, and observations need to stay connected with the material they describe.
At OIST, I helped set up the fish collection and developed protocols that students can use as they learn preparation and molecular workflows. I am also building three-dimensional specimen models to connect with genomic datasets.
I plan to share these models and genomic resources online so researchers can work with the data remotely. Making specimen information easier to reach is especially valuable for colleagues who face financial or geographic barriers to visiting collections, including researchers in the Global South.

title: Teaching & Mentoring
text:
One of the things I enjoy most about research is helping someone work through a question and reach a point where they can decide what to try next. That might mean learning to identify a fish, troubleshooting a DNA extraction, or figuring out what a statistical result actually tells us.
I have been the primary research mentor for more than 20 trainees. My experience includes two master’s thesis students through Northeastern University’s Three Seas Program. Many trainees have contributed to papers, presented at conferences, and continued into PhD programs.

title: Teaching & Mentoring
text:
How I work with students

Start with the question
I encourage students to keep asking what they are trying to learn and why a particular method will help. Learning a technique is valuable, and understanding when to use it makes that skill much more transferable.
Projects usually involve a mixture of practical work, reading, discussion, and analysis. I help students break an unfamiliar task into manageable steps, then give them room to make decisions as their experience grows.


Make room for learning
People arrive with different backgrounds, and I want students to feel comfortable saying that something is new to them. Several interns I trained began without molecular experience. By the end of their internships, each had processed more than 100 specimens and produced DNA extractions suitable for whole-genome sequencing.
That progress takes clear instructions, practice, useful feedback, and time to troubleshoot. I want students to recognize what they have learned as well as what they still want to work on.


Think beyond one project
A research experience is also a chance to explore what kind of work someone enjoys. I make time for conversations about careers, further study, collaborations, and ways to communicate research.
My aim is for students to leave with skills they can use independently, a better sense of their interests, and people they can continue turning to for advice. I value the relationships that last after a project ends.

title: Phylogenetics & Biogeography
text:
Maps and evolutionary trees offer different views of biodiversity. I bring them together to investigate where fish lineages occur, how their distributions developed, and what their anatomy and ecology can tell us about those histories.
Much of this work centers on goatfishes. Projects with wrasses and damselfishes let me explore related questions in other groups.

title: Phylogenetics & Biogeography
text:
Getting to know goatfishes
Goatfishes search for food with a pair of sensory barbels beneath the jaw. Watching them feed raises questions about how anatomy, movement, and substrate use fit together.
During my doctorate, I worked on their evolutionary relationships alongside specimen-based morphology and feeding observations in Moorea. The resulting phylogeny gives these organismal comparisons a historical framework.
In Nash et al. (2022), we resolved relationships among 72 species and dated their most recent common ancestor to around 22 million years ago. The tree showed a sharp increase in lineage accumulation around five million years ago. Body shape was strongly structured by evolutionary relationships, suggesting a useful starting point for investigating recent species differences within older morphological lineages.
The goatfish phylogeny paper

title: Phylogenetics & Biogeography
text:
Describing ranges that overlap
A widespread species can belong to several regional assemblages. Assigning it one geographic label loses some of that information.
I became interested in describing geographic occupancy as a set of proportions. The idea connects with compositional analysis, an approach used in fields including microbiology. Because proportions sum to a whole, their dependence needs to be included in the analysis.
Using that framework, I combined more than 100,000 occurrence records with the goatfish phylogeny and morphology. It allowed me to estimate past geographic compositions and compare evolutionary models while retaining the overlap among distributions.

What emerged
The analysis recovered a clear Atlantic–Indo-Pacific divide and distinct regional assemblages. Range size and morphology had weak associations with geographic composition. Evolutionary models nevertheless supported repeated convergence toward particular compositional states.
The interesting next step is to ask what produces those recurring patterns. Similar geographic distributions might reflect similar ecological associations, continuing exchange among populations, or quite different histories.
The manuscript is under review at Systematic Biology.

title: Phylogenetics & Biogeography
text:
Other lineages, related questions

Wrasses and parrotfishes
Different parts of a genome can support different evolutionary trees. I contributed analyses and writing to Hughes et al. (2023), which examined relationships and phylogenomic discordance in wrasses and parrotfishes.
Read the study


Damselfishes
For McCord et al. (2021), I carried out the diversification analyses, examining associations with feeding ecology and body size using multistate hidden-state speciation and extinction models.
Medium-sized species and pelagic planktivores had the highest estimated net diversification rates. The contrast with some broader reef-fish results is one reason I am interested in checking how well evolutionary associations carry across lineages.
Read the study

title: Phylogenetics & Biogeography
text:
Looking within species
Comparative datasets often represent a species with one value for a trait. My population work offers a way to ask how much depends on that choice.
I want to compare populations across a species’ range, assess how conclusions change with the populations included, and develop analyses that retain more of that variation. This connects my interest in large geographic patterns with the smaller-scale differences we can observe in specimens and living fishes.

title: Traits & Communities
text:
A fish community can be described as a list of species, a collection of body shapes, or a set of ecological traits. I am interested in how those descriptions relate to one another.
My work combines videos of living fishes with trait data, specimen measurements, and evolutionary information. I use those different views to investigate variation among habitats and among populations of the same species.

title: Traits & Communities
text:
Neighbors at Diamond Beach
At Diamond Beach in Seragaki, Onna, Okinawa, seagrass, rubble, and coral habitats occur close together. This provides an opportunity to compare the fishes found in neighboring parts of the same reef landscape.
We collected 44 one-hour unattended videos at eight permanent stations on two cross-shore transects. We used the recordings to identify species and combined those observations with ecological traits and geometric morphometrics.

Species changed more than measured traits
We recorded 146 species, with complete trait information for 141 species representing 97.9% of recorded occurrences.
Richness increased toward coral habitats, and species composition differed markedly across the habitat gradient. The replacement of measured trait space was much smaller than species replacement: the mean pairwise functional-to-taxonomic replacement ratio among zones was approximately 0.16.



What the overlap leaves open
Different assemblages often contained fishes with similar broad trait profiles. Those profiles leave room for differences in feeding behavior, resource use, interactions, and responses to environmental change.
I want to investigate those finer differences. Similarity in measured traits alone does not demonstrate that species perform identical functions or compensate for one another after a disturbance.
The first-author manuscript is in preparation, with submission planned by December 2026.

title: Traits & Communities
text:
Looking across species
A longer-term question is whether species found together show corresponding geographic patterns.
If several species share genetic breaks, I can investigate whether they also show similar morphological differences. If their shapes vary in similar ways despite different population histories, that would motivate closer examination of shared ecological conditions.
Comparing several lineages at the same places helps identify patterns worth testing more broadly. I also want to explore how this variation within species can be carried into comparative studies of trait evolution and diversification.

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
An island on a map is a convenient place to collect fishes. Whether it corresponds to a genetic population is a question to test.
I use genomic data to investigate connections among islands and compare the histories of species found in the same region. My main project is based in the Ryukyus, with roots in earlier work on Caribbean silversides.

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
Following the Kuroshio Current
The Kuroshio Current carries warm water northward alongside the Ryukyu Archipelago, where many tropical fishes approach the northern limits of their distributions. That combination makes the region especially interesting for studying dispersal and establishment.
I want to know whether connections to southern biodiversity sources help explain the diversity of these communities. I am also interested in how continued exchange might contribute to replenishment after local losses. Typhoons, coastal modification, fishing, and the region’s history of warfare add important context to questions about persistence and recovery.
The genomic work can help identify connections and reconstruct population histories. Testing replenishment and resilience will also require ecological observations.

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
Comparing seven fishes
I designed a sampling program for seven reef fishes that differ in diet, water-column position, and social strategies. Sampling spans six locations:

Tanegashima
Amami Oshima
Okinawa Honto
Miyakojima
Ishigaki
Kumejima




Study Design


Comparing species along the same island chain helps investigate which genetic patterns they share and which are associated with their different characteristics.
The work combines market sampling and targeted collecting with local fisheries cooperatives. Preserved specimens, tissues, and locality records keep each genetic sample connected to an identifiable fish and collecting event.

Project progress
The figures below reflect progress as of November 2026.







Component
Current status

More than 600 collected

Seven completed

Sampling continues, and coverage is still uneven among species and places. I am developing the morphological dataset alongside the genetic work so the same individuals can be compared in more than one way.

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
What we are finding

Testing island-based expectations
COI haplotype networks showed that Okinawa samples did not form an exclusive island-specific cluster. That observation prompted questions about shared ancestry, continuing exchange, and historical colonization.
Mitochondrial data alone cannot distinguish those explanations. Population-structure, gene-flow, and demographic analyses are underway using the genome-wide data.


Looking closely at species identities
COI and whole-genome differentiation supports two species among fishes currently identified as Parupeneus barberinus. This raises questions about the distributions and ecological associations represented within its nominal range.
A related project examines species boundaries and possible hybridization in Pterocaesio. These findings and questions make taxonomy an important part of interpreting the connectivity data.


Comparing diversity
Preliminary analyses suggest higher genetic diversity in the Okinawa samples than at other sampled locations. More balanced sampling is needed before interpreting that difference confidently.

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
An earlier island project
My early marine research focused on Atherinomorus stipes, the hardhead silverside, among islands in Belize and the Florida Keys.
In Nash et al. (2017), we found high mitochondrial haplotype diversity and distinct regional lineages, with no support for isolation by distance within the sampled island groups. That work helped shape my interest in how habitat associations and history influence genetic structure.
The Ryukyu project lets me revisit these questions across several species with much broader genomic data.
The silverside paper

title: Population Genomics & Connectivity
text:
Future avenues
Comparisons with samples from Taiwan, the Philippines, and other potential source areas would help test the timing and direction of exchange. I also want to ask whether fishes with similar connections share ecological characteristics, and whether population histories line up with differences in body shape and habitat use.
Over time, pairing genetic analyses with recruitment monitoring could help evaluate whether connected populations show stronger replenishment following local declines.

title: Research
text:
I study fishes to understand how geography, ecology, and evolutionary history fit together. A species can occur across an enormous stretch of ocean, with populations living among different habitats and neighbors. I want to know what makes that possible and how much those populations differ.
My projects connect observations made underwater with specimens, DNA, three-dimensional models, and evolutionary trees. Some focus on individual populations, others on entire fish families or local communities. Moving between these scales helps me find connections that a single approach might miss.

title: Research
text:
Evolutionary trees and geographic distributions

How do lineages come to occupy different parts of the ocean?
Goatfishes have been a starting point for much of my work. I use their evolutionary relationships, feeding biology, body shapes, and geographic records to investigate the history of their diversity.
One question led me to borrow an idea from compositional analysis: instead of assigning a widespread species to one region, describe how its distribution is divided among regions. That creates new ways to compare geographic histories and look for recurring patterns.
Collaborations on wrasses and damselfishes let me explore related questions in other groups, including disagreements among gene trees and associations between ecological traits and diversification.
Explore phylogenetics and biogeography →

title: Research
text:
Population genomics and connectivity

What connects fish populations across islands?
My current work in Japan compares seven reef fishes across a shared island setting. I use genomic data to investigate exchange among populations, differences in genetic diversity, and changes in population size through time.
The Kuroshio Current makes the Ryukyus an especially interesting place to ask these questions. I am testing whether species experience similar connections along the archipelago or whether their ecological differences are associated with different histories.
This work builds on my early research with Caribbean silversides and expands those questions to multiple lineages and genome-wide data.
Explore population genomics →

title: Research
text:
Morphology and communities

What changes when the species in a habitat change?
At Diamond Beach in Okinawa, nearby seagrass, rubble, and coral habitats contain markedly different fish assemblages. My community research examines how much ecological-trait diversity changes alongside species identity.
I am also using photogrammetry to build three-dimensional models of fishes sampled for genomic research. These linked datasets will help investigate whether species found together show similar geographic differences in morphology and genetic structure.
Explore traits and communities →

title: Research
text:
Bringing the projects together
A recurring interest across my work is variation within species. I want to understand how conclusions about ecology and evolution change when we look beyond a single representative specimen, population, or species average.
Collections make that possible across a much wider geographic area than fieldwork alone. Combining historical and contemporary specimens with ecological observations and genomic data gives me different ways to investigate why fishes live where they do and how their diversity has developed.
I enjoy the analytical side of this work, especially when a question sends me looking for an unfamiliar method or a useful connection to another field.

title: Chloe M. Nash, PhD
text:
Hello, I’m Chloe!
I’m a Postdoctoral Scholar in the Macroevolution Unit at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST). I study marine fishes, with interests that range from behavior to the history of an entire lineage. I completed my PhD in 2023 under the supervision of Dr. Mark Westneat in the Committee on Evolutionary Biology at the University of Chicago.
I study how populations of widespread fishes vary across habitats and ecological communities. By combining field observations, museum specimens, genomic data, and body-shape measurements, I investigate how connectivity and environmental differences shape variation within species and what these patterns reveal about their evolutionary histories.
My projects have taken me from Caribbean silversides to goatfishes in French Polynesia and reef fishes in Japan. I enjoy the combination of time underwater, careful specimen work, and analytical problems that send me looking for a new approach.
Away from research, I like diving, finding a good cafe, and listening to live music.

Goatfishes use sensory barbels beneath the jaw to search for food. Their anatomy and feeding behavior offer plenty of questions about how fishes use different environments.
My work brings together feeding observations, body shape, evolutionary relationships, and geographic distributions. It has also led me to explore different ways of describing ranges that overlap across regions.

Reef neighbors at Diamond Beach

I am interested in what those broad similarities leave open, including finer differences in feeding, habitat use, and responses to environmental conditions.

title: Chloe M. Nash, PhD
section: In the field and in collections
text:
In the field and in collections
Fieldwork gives me opportunities to observe living fishes and learn from local researchers and fishers. Collections keep those observations connected to specimens that can be studied again as new questions and methods emerge.
At OIST, I helped establish the fish collection and develop preparation and cataloging workflows. I am building resources that connect specimens with tissues, photographs, three-dimensional models, and genomic data, with plans to share models and genomic resources online.

title: Chloe M. Nash, PhD
text:
Learning together
Working with students is a part of research I particularly enjoy. I help trainees build practical and analytical skills while finding questions they want to pursue. I also value the conversations about careers, collaboration, and learning that continue after a project ends.
Teaching and mentoring →

title: Collections & Natural History
text:
Collections let me return to an observation, compare fishes from places I cannot sample myself, and ask new questions of material collected years earlier. I enjoy that cumulative part of research: someone else’s careful collecting can make a project possible, and material I prepare today may become useful in ways I have not yet considered.
My work involves both using collections and helping build them. I am interested in keeping the connections among a fish, its tissues, its collecting locality, and the different datasets that come from studying it.

title: Collections & Natural History
section: What stays connected to a specimen?
text:
What stays connected to a specimen?
A collection record brings several kinds of evidence together. Each adds something different to what we can investigate.







Resource
What it contributes




Preserved fish
Identification, external morphology, and anatomy


Suitably preserved tissues
Genetic diversity, relationships, and population history


Photographs and three-dimensional models
Visual records and opportunities to examine external form remotely


Locality and date
Geographic and historical context


Habitat notes and field observations
Information about the setting and behavior of living fishes



Keeping those links clear makes it easier to revisit an identification, compare results across methods, or find material for a different project.

title: Collections & Natural History
section: Building the fish collection at OIST
text:
Building the fish collection at OIST
I helped establish OIST’s fish collection as part of my Ryukyu research. The connectivity project has produced more than 600 specimens through fish-market sampling and targeted collecting. Vouchers and tissues are held at OIST or planned for deposition in regional museums, including the Kagoshima University Museum.
I created a cataloging system and developed protocols for specimen preparation, fixation, and DNA extraction. This work includes training students to carry samples through the different steps while keeping labels, records, and associated material connected.
It has also made the practical side of collections especially important to me. A field trip creates work that continues through preparation, documentation, storage, and future access to the material.
Fieldwork and collecting →

title: Collections & Natural History
text:
Bringing specimens into three dimensions
For fishes included in my Ryukyu genomics study, I am generating three-dimensional models through photogrammetry. The process uses photographs to reconstruct a specimen’s external surface.
These models will add another way to examine the same individuals represented in the genomic data. I want to use the paired information to investigate geographic differences in shape and how those differences relate to ecology and population history.
I plan to release the models and genomic resources through open repositories, together with the information needed to connect them to their specimens. Online access can make collection-based work more practical for researchers facing travel costs or geographic barriers, including colleagues in the Global South.
Morphology and community research →

title: Collections & Natural History
text:
Older specimens, new comparisons
Historical collections extend the places and times available for comparison. They can help investigate body-shape variation, check geographic records, or identify locations where new sampling would be useful.
I am interested in combining these holdings with contemporary collecting and ecological observations. The comparisons require attention to identification, locality information, life stage, and preservation, as well as whether associated material is suitable for a particular analysis.
This is one way my interests in natural history and quantitative biology come together: a useful analysis starts with understanding the organisms and the records behind the dataset.

title: Collections & Natural History
text:
Working with digital biodiversity records
My goatfish research has involved compiling more than 300,000 occurrence records from sources including GBIF, VertNet, and OBIS. These resources make it possible to investigate distributions far beyond the places I have visited.
Working with them also involves checking names, localities, duplicates, and the evidence supporting a record. An unusual occurrence can be worth investigating, whether it points to an identification problem, a geographic error, or a potentially informative observation.
I want digital records to remain traceable to specimens or observations wherever possible. That makes geographic analyses easier to evaluate and gives other researchers a route back to the underlying evidence.
Biogeography research →

title: Collections & Natural History
text:
Resources that outlast a project
My goal is to leave material and records that other people can use. That includes physical specimens, well-documented tissues, digital models, and genomic datasets, alongside the local partnerships that make collecting possible.
I work with regional researchers, fishers, fisheries cooperatives, and museums to keep questions about deposition, data use, recognition, and access part of the collaboration. Building a useful collection is an ongoing relationship with both the material and the people who contribute to it.
